# Gaussian Representation and Truncation
Also called: 3DGS Representation, Gaussian Representation and Rendering
## Overview
This family extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by modifying the density function, truncation logic, texture mapping, or proliferation strategy to address specific rendering and optimization limitations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting](13138-discontinuity-aware-gaussian-splatting.md) and [Appearance and Physical Modeling](15766-appearance-and-physical-modeling.md) by focusing on primitive representation, culling thresholds, and training-time densification constraints rather than post-processing transformations or neural field substitutions.
## Shared principles
## Subtopics

### [Inverse Multiquadric Splatting](9910-inverse-multiquadric-splatting.md)
Replaces the standard Gaussian density function with an inverse multiquadric radial basis function to modify alpha blending behavior. It sets itself apart from base 3DGS by using a function with heavier tails, which can improve the representation of certain geometric structures or reduce artifacts in specific optimization scenarios. Choose it when standard Gaussian tails cause artifacts or insufficient coverage of geometric structures.

### [Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation](10266-opacity-independent-gaussian-truncation.md)
Modifies the fragment culling logic to decouple the visibility threshold from the Gaussian's opacity parameter. It sets itself apart from siblings like [Pruning and Reduction](14909-pruning-and-reduction.md) by modifying the runtime rendering loop's culling condition rather than post-processing the Gaussian set, and from [Inverse Multiquadric Splatting](9910-inverse-multiquadric-splatting.md) by retaining the Gaussian density function while altering its evaluation threshold. Choose it when low-opacity Gaussians fail to optimize consistently or when aggressive spatial truncation is required.

### [Content-Aware Texturing for Gaussian Splatting](12606-content-aware-texturing-for-gaussian-splatting.md)
Augments 2D Gaussian primitives with spatially varying texture maps to capture high-frequency appearance details that fixed spherical harmonics cannot represent. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by dynamically allocating texture resolution based on local image content and error, avoiding the convergence issues associated with cloning-based densification. Choose it for scenes requiring high-frequency appearance details without convergence issues from primitive cloning.

### [Directed Distance Field (DDF) for Gaussian Splatting](12854-directed-distance-field-ddf-for-gaussian-splatting.md)
A neural implicit representation that serves as a constant-time, constant-memory ray oracle for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It maps a ray origin and direction to the distance to the first surface and a visibility probability, enabling efficient secondary ray queries for shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination without requiring a mesh or traversing a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). It sets itself apart from sibling methods that scale with the number of Gaussians, as the DDF’s query cost and memory footprint remain fixed regardless of scene size. Choose it when efficient secondary ray queries are needed without mesh extraction or BVH traversal.

### [Atomized Proliferation](12935-atomized-proliferation.md)
A training optimization strategy that enhances geometric precision by constraining Gaussians representing fine details into "Atom Gaussians" (isotropic spheroids with uniform size) and prioritizing their proliferation to align with scene geometry, followed by pruning to merge large smooth surfaces. It sets itself apart from siblings like [Pruning and Reduction](14909-pruning-and-reduction.md) by actively restructuring the Gaussian population into isotropic atoms for fine details while retaining larger anisotropic Gaussians for smooth backgrounds, rather than simply removing low-impact primitives. Choose it when strict geometric alignment and uniform detail coverage are prioritized over free-form Gaussian drift.

### [Pruning and Reduction](14909-pruning-and-reduction.md)
Removes redundant or low-impact 3D Gaussians from a trained or training model to reduce memory footprint and rendering latency while preserving visual fidelity. Unlike sibling methods that focus on geometric simplification of primitives or opacity-independent truncation, this family focuses on the selection and elimination of entire Gaussian entities based on their contribution to the rendered image or their geometric degeneracy. It is distinct from [Gaussian Representation and Truncation](12855-gaussian-representation-and-truncation.md) by actively modifying the set of Gaussians $\{G_i\}$ rather than just their rendering parameters. Choose it when memory reduction and rendering latency are critical without altering the core representation or culling logic.

### POG (Potentially Over-large Gaussians)
POG improves LPIPS slightly but degrades PSNR significantly compared to Hard Gaussians (HG) [S2]. POG overgrows already learned areas, making them susceptible to redundant Gaussians, which causes PSNR degradation [S2]. Tanks&Temples ablation results show POG yields PSNR 26.26, SSIM 0.879, LPIPS 0.121, while HG yields PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126 [S2].

### View-Dependent Opacity Kernel
A transparent Gaussian kernel where opacity is view-dependent, modeled by a half-period cosine function to approximate specular reflectance lobes [S3, unofficial]. It adds 5 learnable parameters to the standard 3DGS configuration [S3, unofficial]. The opacity is defined as:
$$ \hat{\alpha}(\theta, \beta, T, \alpha) = \alpha \cdot \frac{\cos(\max(0, \min(\frac{2\theta}{T}, \pi)))+1}{2}\exp(\beta) $$
where $\alpha$ is the base opacity, $\theta$ is the angle between view direction and lobe central orientation, $T$ controls angular span, and $\beta$ modulates sharpness [S3, unofficial]. $T$ is initialized as $c\bar{\theta}_i/\pi$ based on viewpoint density, and $\beta$ is initialized to zero [S3, unofficial]. If $\theta$ increases, transparency diminishes to zero, ensuring minimal impact on viewpoints outside the lobe's influence and preventing artifacts [S3, unofficial].

### GS-IR Representation
GS-IR extends the vanilla 3D Gaussian representation by adding a normal vector and material properties to the geometric and appearance parameters [S4]. Geometric properties $T$ are defined as a set containing position vector $p$, scaling vector $s$, unit quaternion $q$ for rotation, and normal vector $n$ [S4]. Material properties $M$ are defined as a set containing albedo $a$, roughness $\rho$, and metallicity $m$ [S4]. Vanilla 3D Gaussian appearance parameters $A$ consist of opacity $\alpha$ and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients $f_c$ for view-dependent color [S4].

## Background
Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) introduced Potentially Over-large Gaussians and Hard Gaussians to address blurring and needle-like artifacts [S2]. AtomGS introduced Atomized Proliferation and Geometry-Guided Optimization for high-fidelity radiance fields [S2]. Augmented Radiance Field introduced View-Dependent Opacity Kernels for specular reflectance [S3, unofficial]. GS-IR extended the representation for inverse rendering with material properties [S4].
